name: Scientific Figure Generator
tagline: Turns text, abstracts or rough sketches into scientific diagrams and graphical abstracts you can drop into a paper.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The architecture is not the hard part: a model that emits SVG, a canvas that renders it, and a chat box that feeds edits back in is a weekend of work. The hard part is that generic models produce diagrams that look like generic models produced them, with drifting label alignment, muddled arrows and typography a reviewer will notice. A personal build gets you to 'readable in a lab meeting' quickly and then stalls well short of 'figure 3 in a submitted manuscript', and you will spend the saved money's worth of evenings nudging coordinates. If your figures are mostly boxes, arrows and flows, build it. If they are cell biology scenes that need a curated icon library, you are not building that in a sitting.
coreLoopDIY: Local web app where you paste an abstract or sketch description, get a rendered SVG figure back from an LLM, then refine it through a chat loop and export to SVG, PNG or PDF.
requirements: An API key for a frontier model with vision, in .env
Local font files if you care about matching a journal's typography
Willingness to hand-edit SVG when the model puts a label through an arrow
whatYouLose: A curated, scientifically accurate icon and glyph library, which is the actual bottleneck for biology and chemistry figures
Layout polish: consistent spacing, aligned baselines, arrows that terminate where they should
Journal-ready export presets, DPI and color space handling
Fast iteration without burning tokens on every tweak
Someone else's taste, which is doing more work in these tools than people admit
moatNotes: The defensible asset in this category has historically been the asset library and the layout taste around it, not the model call.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a figure is a deadline artifact. When you are three days from submission you do not want to debug SVG transforms, you want something that renders cleanly, exports at the right resolution and does not make a reviewer squint. The chat-to-edit loop existing at all is cheap; it existing and producing something that holds up at print size is the thing being charged for, and that comes from tuning nobody writes down.
notes: Build it if your figures are flowcharts in a lab coat; buy it if they need actual biology icons.
prompt:
Build a local-only web app called FigureForge that turns research text into editable scientific figures.

Stack, no substitutions: Vite + React + TypeScript on the front end, a small Express server in the same repo for model calls, pnpm, Tailwind for UI chrome only.

Core loop:
1. A left pane with a textarea: user pastes an abstract, a methods paragraph or a plain-language description of a sketch. A file input accepts one image (a photo of a whiteboard or hand sketch).
2. On submit, the server calls the Anthropic Messages API (key in .env as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, never hardcoded) with a system prompt that instructs the model to return ONLY a complete, standalone SVG document: viewBox set, no external fonts, no raster images, no scripts.
3. The right pane renders that SVG inline and nothing else. No iframe.
4. Below the render, a chat input. Each follow-up message sends the current SVG source plus the instruction back to the model and asks for the full revised SVG. Keep the last 10 revisions in memory with a version dropdown so the user can roll back when an edit makes things worse.
5. A source toggle shows the raw SVG in a CodeMirror editor; edits there update the render immediately and become the new current version.

Export: buttons for SVG download, PNG at a user-chosen scale (1x to 6x) via canvas rasterization, and PDF via svg2pdf.js + jsPDF. Default PNG scale 4x.

In scope: box-and-arrow diagrams, flowcharts, pipelines, timelines, simple plots drawn as SVG, panel layouts with A/B/C labels.
Out of scope, and say so in the UI: photorealistic or anatomically accurate biological icons. Add a one-line note telling users to import their own icon set.

Icon support: a /public/icons folder; any SVG dropped there is listed in a sidebar and can be referenced by filename in a prompt, with the server inlining the file contents into the model context.

No accounts, no database, no telemetry, no cloud. State lives in localStorage. Ship a README with setup, the .env example, and a short list of prompts that actually produce decent output.
